name: Kuzu
baseline: Neo4j Community 2025.12.1 (Cypher over Bolt, Python driver)
workload: 30 custom Cypher queries (n-hop traversals with varied cardinalities, filters, projections) on the LDBC SNB SF1 graph (3,181,724 nodes, 17,256,038 relationships), mean latency per query with pytest-benchmark, Python clients; Kuzu 0.11.3 in-process versus Neo4j 2025.12.1 in a VM.
claimed_speedup: Kuzu 0.11.3 has lower mean latency than Neo4j 2025.12.1 on 21 of 30 queries (count derived from page data) and a geometric mean of per-query Neo4j/Kuzu latency ratios of 1.27x (derived from page data: the README gives Ladybug 2.02x and 1.59x over Neo4j and Kuzu). Largest wins: q20 393.291 ms vs 13.666 ms (28.78x), q30 1055.151 ms vs 153.493 ms (6.87x), q8 11.720 ms vs 2.651 ms (4.42x), q6 3.145 ms vs 0.705 ms (4.46x). Kuzu is slower on 9 queries, worst q7 27.588 ms vs 1.508 ms (0.05x), q22 21.507 ms vs 2.618 ms (0.12x), q27 14.305 ms vs 2.518 ms (0.18x), q13 42.157 ms vs 8.398 ms (0.20x). Earlier study by the same author (github.com/prrao87/kuzudb-study, Kuzu 0.9.0 vs Neo4j 2025.03.0, 100K persons / ~2.4M edges, M3 MacBook Pro): ingestion 0.58 s vs 30.64 s (52.8x), query 8 (second-degree paths) 0.0086 s vs 3.2203 s (374.45x), query 9 40.81x, query 1 10.77x, but Kuzu slower on query 5 (0.56x) and query 6 (0.54x).
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt kuzu 0.11.3 Python package (library build compiler and flags not stated); harness: uv run --frozen pytest benchmark_query.py --benchmark-min-rounds=5 --benchmark-warmup-iterations=5 --benchmark-disable-gc, pytest-benchmark 5.2.3, Python 3.13.14.
hardware: Apple M5, 10 logical CPUs, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2; Neo4j ran in a native-arm64 Colima VM with 4 CPUs and 10 GiB RAM, embedded engines ran natively.
tradeoffs: Embedded in-process graph database (no server), property-graph model with a declared schema, Cypher, columnar disk-based storage, CSR adjacency lists, vectorized and factorized processor, multi-threaded query execution. Neo4j is a transactional server. The repository was archived by its owner on 2025-10-10 (read-only; the official extension server is gone, v0.11.3 bundles algo, fts, json and vector); LadybugDB/ladybug is the community continuation.
caveats: Third-party, single-author benchmark (8 stars) on a custom 30-query workload that the README says is not an official LDBC result. Resources are unequal by the author's own note: Neo4j limited to 4 CPUs and 10 GiB in a VM, Kuzu multi-threaded on the native 10-CPU machine, no controlled cold caches. Kuzu loses 9 of 30 queries, and the geometric-mean advantage (1.27x) is far smaller than the headline ratios, which are dominated by q20 and q30. Kuzu's rows come from an earlier run (2026-09-03) than Ladybug's (2026-09-30); sources unchanged on main. Query result conversion is inside the timed region (Python clients). The 100K-person study has Kuzu multi-threaded against single-threaded Neo4j and loads Neo4j through the Python driver instead of admin-import. Kuzu's own blog and docs numbers (kuzudb.github.io) were not reachable here. Build compiler and flags of the prebuilt wheel are not stated, so not tier A.

name: Ladybug
baseline: Neo4j Community 2025.12.1 (Cypher over Bolt, Python driver)
workload: 30 custom Cypher queries (n-hop traversals with varied cardinalities, filters, projections) on the LDBC SNB SF1 graph (3,181,724 nodes, 17,256,038 relationships), mean latency per query with pytest-benchmark, Python clients; Ladybug 0.21.1 in-process versus Neo4j 2025.12.1 in a VM.
claimed_speedup: Ladybug 0.21.1 has lower mean latency than Neo4j 2025.12.1 on 26 of 30 queries; README: geometric mean of per-query Neo4j/Ladybug latency ratios 2.02x (recomputed from the table: 2.02x, derived from page data). Largest wins: q20 393.291 ms vs 14.118 ms (27.86x), q30 1055.151 ms vs 88.728 ms (11.89x), q4 3.141 ms vs 0.382 ms (8.22x), q1 4.098 ms vs 1.171 ms (3.50x). Ladybug is slower on 4 queries: q7 23.600 ms vs 1.508 ms (0.06x), q22 7.134 ms vs 2.618 ms (0.37x), q12 7.708 ms vs 3.888 ms (0.50x), q27 3.492 ms vs 2.518 ms (0.72x). README also reports a 1.59x geometric-mean advantage over Kuzu 0.11.3.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt ladybug 0.21.1 Python package (library build compiler and flags not stated); harness: uv run --frozen pytest benchmark_query.py --benchmark-min-rounds=5 --benchmark-warmup-iterations=5 --benchmark-disable-gc, pytest-benchmark 5.2.3, Python 3.13.14; ANALYZE and six ART secondary indexes enabled.
hardware: Apple M5, 10 logical CPUs, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2; Neo4j ran in a native-arm64 Colima VM with 4 CPUs and 10 GiB RAM, embedded engines ran natively.
tradeoffs: Same design as Kuzu: embedded in-process, declared schema, Cypher, columnar storage, vectorized and factorized joins, multi-threaded. Neo4j is a transactional server, so the comparison is analytical read queries only. Bindings for Python, Node.js, Rust, Go, Swift and Java live in separate repositories.
caveats: Same codebase as kuzudb/kuzu (README: 'formerly known as Kuzu'; a community continuation of the archived project, not a GitHub-level fork), so the evidence overlaps the Kuzu entry; fold or keep per orchestrator policy. Third-party, single-author benchmark (8 stars) on a custom workload that the README says is not an official LDBC result; the author wrote the earlier Kuzu study and any tie to LadybugDB is not established. Resources are unequal by the README's own note (Neo4j 4 CPUs and 10 GiB in a VM, embedded engines native and multi-threaded), no controlled cold caches. Ladybug was re-run on 2026-09-30 while Neo4j and Kuzu values come from earlier runs (2026-09-03) on the same machine. Result conversion is inside the timed region. Open Ladybug issue #1117 reports a two-hop traversal regression since 0.21. A 2026 arXiv preprint (2609.23315, per a search snippet only, page blocked here) reportedly gives Ladybug 3.97 ms vs Neo4j 6.92 ms query-latency geometric mean at 1.02M nodes; not verified. Build compiler and flags of the prebuilt wheel are not stated, so not tier A.

name: libpg_query
baseline: sqlparser-rs (Rust SQL parser, sqlparser crate 0.52, MySQL dialect rows)
workload: Parse-only latency of single statements (simple SELECT, SELECT with JOIN, complex SELECT with GROUP BY/HAVING/ORDER BY/LIMIT, INSERT VALUES, BEGIN) through pg_query_raw_parse (Google Benchmark) versus sqlparser-rs Parser::parse_sql (Criterion), as measured in the ParserSQL project's comparison harness.
claimed_speedup: pg_query_raw_parse vs sqlparser-rs, reference results table: simple SELECT 684 ns vs 4,687 ns (6.9x, derived from page data), SELECT JOIN 1,646 ns vs 10,684 ns (6.5x, derived), complex SELECT 3,304 ns vs 23,411 ns (7.1x, derived), INSERT 781 ns vs 3,784 ns (4.8x, derived), BEGIN 230 ns vs 412 ns (1.8x, derived). With the public pg_query_parse JSON output: simple SELECT 1,872 ns vs 4,687 ns (2.5x, derived), complex SELECT 8,675 ns vs 23,411 ns (2.7x, derived), but BEGIN 421 ns vs 412 ns (parity).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3 -O3 for libpg_query (Makefile default CFLAGS_OPT_LEVEL = -O3) and for the Google Benchmark harness (bench/bench_comparison.cpp); sqlparser-rs through cargo bench (criterion 0.5.1, sqlparser 0.52, bench/sqlparser_rs_bench), Rust release profile.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, Linux 6.17 (reference results in REPRODUCING.md; docs/benchmarks/latest.md confirms the CPU and g++ 13.3.0).
tradeoffs: Extracts the real PostgreSQL parser (Bison grammar, lexer, node types, memory contexts) into a standalone C library, so it accepts PostgreSQL syntax exactly but only PostgreSQL syntax. The public API pays for JSON or Protobuf serialization on top of the raw parse (about 2.7x the raw parse time in this harness); the raw parse API is internal. The 18-latest branch uses upb for Protobuf (changelog: substantially faster than protobuf-c, no numbers).
caveats: Not a libpg_query claim: the numbers come from a rival project's harness (ProxySQL/ParserSQL, 4 stars, agent instruction files in the repo), where libpg_query is the baseline being beaten (ParserSQL is 3.1x faster on parse-only, 8.4x with JSON). The libpg_query claim here is the derived ratio against sqlparser-rs. The sqlparser-rs rows are the MySQL-dialect benchmark (sqlparser_rs_mysql_* names) on statements that are valid in both dialects; libpg_query was cloned at HEAD without a pin and the README figures differ from the REPRODUCING.md table (ParserSQL simple SELECT 178 ns vs 223 ns), so the numbers are version-dependent. I did not run the benchmark; the table values were read from the committed page. libpg_query's own benchmark/ directory (README, bench_protobuf.c, microbench_protobuf.c) benchmarks only the Protobuf layer and publishes no results. A PgDog blog post (search snippet only) reports 5x faster parsing by replacing Protobuf with direct C-to-Rust bindings, which concerns the binding layer, not the parser.
